1184.title: The young teacher under the banyan
1184.hook: old sages sit before a young, silent teacher under a banyan, and Yoga names the teacher of the first teachers
1184.carry: ishvara: the teacher of the first teachers
1184.tomorrow: a king gives up his throne, then can't stop thinking about a fawn. where does it lead?
1184.howItsDone: Many Hindu students begin a lesson in scripture, music or dance by chanting Om and bowing to the guru parampara, the line of teachers, and Guru Purnima is kept each year to honor teachers; in the Yoga Sutras, devotion to Ishvara, the teacher of even the earliest teachers, is one way toward stillness.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ratnakara walked home and asked, and Yoga said: see where harm ends, then cultivate its opposite. Today, a question about teachers.
screen: `CULTIVATE THE OPPOSITE.` · `A QUESTION ABOUT TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Under a great banyan tree, the old story goes, four sages sit. They are old and white-haired, wise already, and they still carry doubts they can't untie. Facing them sits their teacher, and he's young. Barely more than a boy. He doesn't say a word. And one by one, as they sit in his silence, their doubts fall away. An old verse, still chanted, calls it a wonder: the students are old, the teacher is young, and the teaching is silence. The teacher is Shiva, as Dakshinamurti, the one who faces south.
screen: `UNDER THE BANYAN.` → `OLD STUDENTS, A YOUNG TEACHER.` → `THE TEACHING IS SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Dakshinamurti is honored as the first teacher, and you can find him on the south-facing wall of many Shiva temples, especially in South India, sitting under his tree. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras make the same move in philosophy. Stillness can come, he says, through devotion to Ishvara, the Lord. And Ishvara is a particular purusha, a witness never touched by the afflictions, by actions or by their ripening. Then the line that answers the banyan. Ishvara is the teacher of even the earliest teachers, because time doesn't limit him. Every teacher had a teacher. At the top of the line, Yoga places one who never had to be a beginner. This is where Yoga parts from Samkhya: Samkhya's count, as we heard it, left no place for a Lord, and Yoga keeps the same map and sets Ishvara above it. Then Patanjali gives the way to reach him: his word is Om. Repeat it, and dwell on its meaning. This isn't only theory. It's a living Hindu habit. Before a lesson in the Veda, in music or in dance, many teachers chant Om and bow to the guru parampara, the line of teachers, often in a verse that begins with Shiva or Narayana and ends with my own teacher. Students touch the teacher's feet. One full moon each year, Guru Purnima, is kept for honoring teachers. You're never learning from just one person. You're joining a line that, for the tradition, starts with the Lord.
screen: `DAKSHINAMURTI: THE FIRST TEACHER.` · `TEACHER OF THE EARLIEST TEACHERS.` · `YOGA ADDS A LORD TO THE MAP.` · `OM, AND THE LINE OF TEACHERS.` · then, large: `IT STARTS WITH THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that stuck, then the person who taught them, if you know, and let the line run back as far as it goes. Bow your head a little to the whole line. If you pray, say Om softly a few times, as the sutras describe, and dwell on its meaning. If you don't, say thank you once for each teacher you can name.
Yoga. The school that keeps Samkhya's map and adds Ishvara, the teacher of even the earliest teachers, whose word is Om.

1185.title: The king and the fawn
1185.hook: King Bharata raises an orphaned fawn until it fills his mind, and Yoga names the groove: samskara
1185.carry: samskara: what you repeat, you become
1185.tomorrow: a great archer drops his bow and weeps. what does Krishna call yoga?
1185.howItsDone: Hindus practice japa, repeating a divine name, often on a mala of 108 beads, and many families chant God's name at a deathbed; teachers of the Yoga Sutras explain why steady repetition matters: each round lays down a new samskara, a trace in the mind.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Yoga, Dakshinamurti under the banyan, and Ishvara: the teacher of the first teachers, whose word is Om. Today, a king, a fawn, and a groove in the mind.
screen: `THE FIRST TEACHER.` · `A GROOVE IN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: King Bharata has given up his throne to live as a hermit by a river, praying. One morning a pregnant doe comes to drink. A lion roars. She leaps the river in terror, her fawn is born in mid-leap and drops into the water, and she dies. Bharata pulls the tiny fawn out and raises it. He feeds it, worries when it wanders, watches the forest for it. Slowly, his prayers fill up with the fawn. And when he dies, the Bhagavata Purana says, his last thought is the fawn. He's born again as a deer.
screen: `A KING BECOMES A HERMIT.` → `A FAWN FROM THE RIVER.` → `HIS LAST THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: But a deer who remembers. He stays near the hermitages, and in his next birth, as a brahmin's son, he guards his mind so carefully that people take him for a simpleton: Jada Bharata, Bharata the dull. The story is a picture of a Yoga word. Samskara: the trace an experience leaves in the mind. Patanjali's word for the mind's movements is vritti, a turning. Vyasa, the Sutras' early commentator, ties them in a wheel. Turnings leave traces, and traces give rise to turnings again. Every thought of the fawn wore Bharata's groove a little deeper, until it was the thought he died with. The Gita says it plainly: whatever a person remembers at the end, they go to, having been absorbed in it. That's why Hindus hope to have God's name on their lips at the end, and why many families chant it at a deathbed. But the wheel turns both ways. Near the end of the first chapter comes the hopeful line: a trace born of true insight blocks the other traces. What wore the old path can wear a new one. That's the reason for so much repetition in Hindu practice: japa on a mala, the same prayer each morning, the same lamp each evening. It isn't empty habit: each round lays a trace you'd be glad to be carried by. And samskara has a second home in Hindu life: the rites that mark a life, from a child's naming to a wedding.
screen: `SAMSKARA: A TRACE.` · `TURNINGS AND TRACES: A WHEEL.` · `WHAT YOU REMEMBER AT THE END.` · `INSIGHT WEARS A NEW PATH.` · then, large: `WHAT YOU REPEAT, YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: Try japa, the way it's done. Count on the joints of your fingers, or on a mala if you have one, and say a divine name slowly, eleven times: Rama, or Om namo Narayanaya, or Om. When the mind wanders down its old path, notice, and come back on the next count. If you don't pray, repeat a word for who you want to become, and count the returns, not the wanderings.
Yoga. Vyasa's wheel: turnings leave traces, traces make turnings, and a trace of insight can wear a new path. Samskara is the trace.

segments.voice: Your line: samskara, what you repeat, you become. Bharata's fawn wore the groove one thought at a time. Until tomorrow.

1186.title: The archer who dropped his bow
1186.hook: Arjuna lets his bow fall in grief at Kurukshetra, and Krishna calls yoga evenness, skill in action, the unjoining from sorrow
1186.tomorrow: caged parrots argue about the Veda at a front door. whose house is it?
1186.howItsDone: Many Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna teaches the grieving Arjuna the yogas of action, knowledge and devotion; in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, posture is one limb among eight, a steady and comfortable seat.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Bharata and the fawn: samskara, what you repeat, you become. Today, our last day with Yoga, and a warrior in tears.
screen: `THE KING AND THE FAWN.` · `AN ARCHER IN TEARS.`

segments.voice: Two armies face each other at Kurukshetra, and the conch shells blow. Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, asks his charioteer to drive into the open ground between them, so he can see who he's about to fight. And he sees his teachers. His grandfather. His cousins and his friends. His limbs go weak, his mouth goes dry, his skin burns. I won't fight, he says. His great bow slips from his hand, and he sinks down in the chariot, overcome with grief. His charioteer is Krishna. What Krishna says next is the Bhagavad Gita.
screen: `TWO ARMIES.` → `HIS TEACHERS, HIS COUSINS.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.`

segments.voice: And the word Krishna reaches for again and again is yoga. Not a pose. In the Gita, yoga is first evenness: do your work standing the same in success and failure, Krishna says; that evenness is called yoga. Two verses later: yoga is skill in action. And in the sixth chapter, a line with a twist: yoga is the unjoining from sorrow, cutting the tie between a person and their pain. Notice what Krishna does with a weeping friend. He doesn't send him home. He teaches him who he really is: the self in every being, the atman, is not killed when the body is killed. Then he teaches him how to act while the heart is heavy. This is karma yoga, the yoga of action: do what's yours to do, as an offering, without clutching at how it turns out. The Gita also speaks of a yoga of knowledge and a yoga of devotion, and Hindu tradition keeps them all. Patanjali's school is one careful version, where posture, asana, is one limb of eight: a seat steady and comfortable enough to look inward. So which is the real yoga? Hindus have never had to choose. But on a hard day, the Gita's meaning is the one close at hand. Many teachers read it this way: yoga isn't feeling nothing. It's not being ruled by the sorrow, so you can still do your part.
screen: `EVENNESS, SKILL IN ACTION.` · `THE UNJOINING FROM SORROW.` · `THE SELF IS NOT KILLED.` · `KNOWLEDGE, DEVOTION, A STEADY SEAT.` · then, large: `YOU CAN STILL DO YOUR PART.`

segments.voice: Sit the way Patanjali describes: steady, not rigid, comfortable, not slumped. Bring to mind one thing that's yours to do this week that feels heavy. Hold it without pushing the feeling away, and let the breath stay even underneath it. If you pray, offer the task to Krishna, or to whatever you pray to, before you begin. If you don't, say quietly: i'll do my part, and let go of how it turns out.
Yoga. In the Gita, evenness of mind, skill in action, and the unjoining from sorrow. In Patanjali, a steady and comfortable seat on the way to stillness.

1187.title: The house where parrots argued
1187.hook: Shankara finds Mandana Mishra's house by its parrots arguing about the Veda, and meets Mimamsa: the meaning is in the doing
1187.carry: mimamsa: the meaning is in the doing
1187.tomorrow: the truth of dharma is hidden in a cave. how do you find it?
1187.howItsDone: Hindu priests and families carry out rites such as the shraddha step by step, in a set order with set words; Mimamsa, the earlier inquiry, is the school that read the Veda's ritual portion as instruction, opening with the desire to know dharma.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna dropped his bow, and Krishna called yoga evenness, even in sorrow. Today, a new school, and a house full of rites.
screen: `AN ARCHER IN TEARS.` · `A NEW SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: A young wandering monk comes to a town on the river Narmada, looking for one man: Mandana Mishra, the great ritual scholar of his day. He asks some women on the road which house is his. They smile. You'll know it, they say. It's the one where the parrots in their cages by the door are arguing about the Veda. Is the Veda its own proof? Do actions bring their own fruit, or does God give it? The monk is Shankara. And when he finally gets inside, Mandana is in the middle of a shraddha, a rite for the ancestors, and he is not pleased to be interrupted.
screen: `LOOKING FOR ONE HOUSE.` → `THE PARROTS ARGUE ABOUT THE VEDA.` → `A RITE, INTERRUPTED.`

segments.voice: The story comes from a later life of Shankara, and it shows what a house soaked in Mimamsa sounded like. Mimamsa means inquiry, careful reflection. Its root text, the Mimamsa Sutras, is credited to the sage Jaimini, and its first line sets the program. Now, therefore, the desire to know dharma. Not God, not the soul, not what the world is made of. Dharma: what is to be done. The Veda has two great parts. The karma kanda, the part about action, holds the hymns and the rites: fire offerings, chants, the exact order of the steps. The jnana kanda, the part about knowledge, holds the Upanishads. Mimamsa reads the first part, and reads it as instruction. A rite isn't a picture of a truth you could just think about instead. Done right, at the right time, in the right order, the doing is the point. In the story, Mandana is irritated to be interrupted mid-rite, and a Mimamsa scholar would understand why: a rite is something asked of you, to be finished as asked. The Brahma Sutras, Vedanta's root text, open almost the same way: the desire to know brahman. So tradition calls Mimamsa the earlier inquiry and Vedanta the later one. And Mimamsa's careful rules for reading instructions shaped how Hindu law books and rites were read for centuries. When a family follows the priest's steps exactly, the sesame, the grass, the water, in order, that seriousness has a long school behind it.
screen: `THE DESIRE TO KNOW DHARMA.` · `KARMA KANDA: THE PART ABOUT ACTION.` · `THE RITE IS AN INSTRUCTION.` · then, large: `THE MEANING IS IN THE DOING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one rite your family keeps: lighting a lamp, a prayer before food, touching an elder's feet, a holiday puja. Walk through it slowly in your mind, step by step, in the order it's done, without judging it. If you pray, do one of those steps for real today, exactly as it was handed to you. If you don't, just notice what the doing asks of you.
Mimamsa. The careful inquiry into dharma, what is to be done, reading the Veda's rites as instruction, where the meaning lives in the doing.

segments.voice: Your line: mimamsa, the meaning is in the doing. Even the parrots knew it. See you tomorrow.

1188.title: The lake of questions
1188.hook: Yudhishthira answers a yaksha by a deadly lake: the truth of dharma is hidden in a cave, and Mimamsa says it's heard, not seen
1188.tomorrow: a generous warrior reaches heaven and is served gold to eat. why?

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mandana Mishra's house, where even the parrots argued about the Veda, and Mimamsa's first line: the desire to know dharma.
screen: `THE DESIRE TO KNOW DHARMA.` · `HOW DO YOU KNOW IT?`

segments.voice: Late in their years of exile, the five Pandava brothers are desperately thirsty. One brother, Nakula, goes looking for water and finds a clear lake. A voice says: answer my questions first, then drink. He drinks anyway, and falls dead. The next brother comes, and the next, and the next. Each ignores the voice, drinks, and falls. Then the eldest, Yudhishthira, arrives, sees his four brothers lying by the water, and doesn't drink. He says: ask. The voice belongs to a yaksha, a powerful spirit, and the questions come fast.
screen: `A CLEAR LAKE.` → `FOUR BROTHERS FALL.` → `THE ELDEST SAYS: ASK.`

segments.voice: One question is the one Mimamsa cared about most. What is the path? Yudhishthira's answer is famous. Argument doesn't settle it. The scriptures differ. No single sage's word is final. The truth of dharma is hidden in a cave. So the path is the one the great have walked. The yaksha is pleased, reveals himself as Dharma, Yudhishthira's own father in disguise, and brings the brothers back to life. Hidden in a cave: Mimamsa makes a close cousin of this point in a philosopher's voice. Jaimini's second sutra: dharma is a good known through codana, the Veda's injunction, its plain do this. Two sutras later he says why. Perception only grasps what's present to the senses, and dharma isn't sitting there in the present to be seen; its good lies in what the act brings about. Film every moment of a shraddha and you'll see sesame, water, rice balls. You won't see the dharma. So where do Hindus find it? Mimamsa says: in the words that ask for it. The law books add more marks: the Veda first, then the remembered teachings, then the conduct of good people, then what sits rightly with your own self. The conduct of good people is Yudhishthira's path, the one the great have walked. It's why, when a child asks why we do this, an honest Hindu answer is often: because it was asked of us, and because the people we trust most did it before us.
screen: `ARGUMENT DOESN'T SETTLE IT.` · `DHARMA, HIDDEN IN A CAVE.` · `KNOWN THROUGH INJUNCTION.` · `HEARD, NOT SEEN.` · then, large: `THE PATH THE GREAT HAVE WALKED.`

1189.title: Karna's plate of gold
1189.hook: Karna is served gold in heaven because he never fed his ancestors, and Mimamsa names what carries an offering on: apurva
1189.tomorrow: a scholar falls from a tower with one word on his lips. which word did he regret?
1189.howItsDone: Hindus offer food and water to the ancestors at shraddha and during Pitru Paksha; Mimamsa teachers, following Shabara, explain that a rite properly done produces apurva, an unseen potency that lasts after the act and brings its result in time.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lake of questions: the truth of dharma is hidden in a cave. Dharma is heard, not seen.
screen: `HEARD, NOT SEEN.` · `THEN WHAT?`

segments.voice: Karna, the warrior famous for never refusing anyone who asked him for anything, dies in battle and rises to heaven. He's hungry, and they bring him food. It's gold. Plates of gold and jewels, and nothing he can eat. He asks why. The answer comes back: on earth you gave gold to everyone, but you never once offered food to your ancestors. Karna had never even known who his ancestors were. So he's allowed back to earth for fifteen days, to offer them food and water. Many families tell this story to explain Pitru Paksha, the fortnight each year for honoring the ancestors.
screen: `A HERO IN HEAVEN.` → `SERVED GOLD, NOT FOOD.` → `FIFTEEN DAYS BACK.`

segments.voice: The story isn't in the Mahabharata itself; it's a popular telling. But it carries a question Mimamsa asked with great care. The Veda says, in effect, the one who desires heaven should perform this offering. Fine. The offering is done. The fire burns down and everyone goes home. The act is finished, gone. But the result it was for comes much later, maybe after this life. How can something that no longer exists bring anything about? Shabara, in his commentary on Jaimini, gives the answer. The act doesn't simply vanish. It produces something unseen, which stays and carries the act forward until its fruit arrives. Its name is apurva: the new thing, something that wasn't there before the act and is there after. You can't film it or prove it by argument. It's known, Mimamsa says, because the Veda asks for the act and promises its fruit. That fits yesterday: dharma couldn't be seen, and apurva is how its good travels through time. Other schools speak of the lasting effect of action in their own ways, and the word karma covers much of that ground. And this shape, an act that ends while what it set moving travels on, is the shape a family trusts at a shraddha. The rice balls are set out. The water is poured. The priest goes home. And Hindus hold that the offering reaches the ones it was made for. Karna came back from heaven to make sure his did.
screen: `THE ACT IS FINISHED.` · `THE FRUIT COMES LATER.` · `APURVA CARRIES IT.` · then, large: `THE OFFERING TRAVELS ON.`

segments.voice: In the spirit of tarpana, the water offering to the ancestors: hold a little water in your cupped right hand, name a grandparent or someone you've lost, and let the water pour out, three times. If you pray, offer it to them with a short prayer. If you don't, simply say their name and thank you, and let the act be complete as an act.
Mimamsa. In Shabara's account, a ritual act produces apurva, an unseen new thing that carries it forward until its fruit comes.

segments.voice: Your line: apurva, the offering travels on. The rite ends; what it set moving doesn't. That's today, done.

1190.title: The scholar who said if
1190.hook: Kumarila falls from a tower crying 'if the Vedas are true', and Mimamsa holds the Veda apaurusheya: heard, never written
1190.carry: apaurusheya: the veda is heard, not written
1190.tomorrow: the fire god runs off with the gods' treasure and weeps silver tears. why tell a story in a book of rules?
1190.howItsDone: Vedic hymns are still learned by ear from a teacher, in recitation patterns that guard every syllable; Mimamsa holds that the Veda is apaurusheya, not authored by any person, which is why its injunctions can be trusted as the way to know dharma.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINETY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Mimamsa, Karna's plate of gold, and apurva: the offering travels on, long after the rite ends.
screen: `THE OFFERING TRAVELS ON.` · `NO AUTHOR.`

segments.voice: A young scholar named Kumarila does something bold. To learn how Buddhist teachers argue against the Veda, he goes to study among them. One day, as his teacher criticizes the Veda, Kumarila weeps, and his secret is out. In the telling, he falls, or is thrown, from the top of a tall tower. As he falls, he cries out: if the Vedas are true, I will live. He lands alive. But he loses one eye. And later he says why. Because of one word. If. For one moment, he had doubted.
screen: `A SCHOLAR IN DISGUISE.` → `IF THE VEDAS ARE TRUE…` → `ONE WORD, ONE EYE.`

segments.voice: The story comes from a later life of Shankara. Kumarila Bhatta was real, one of Mimamsa's greatest thinkers. What would he risk a fall for? The idea at the heart of today. All week, Mimamsa's method has rested on one thing: dharma is known through the Veda's words, and nothing else can see it. So the words had better be reliable. If a person wrote them, a person could be wrong. Jaimini's fifth sutra says the bond between a word and its meaning is original. Nobody invented it. So the Veda's instruction is a true means of knowing dharma, depending on nothing else. Later Mimamsa thinkers, Kumarila among them, spell out the consequence: the Veda is apaurusheya, not made by any person. The rishis didn't compose it. They're called seers; they saw and heard it. That's why the Veda is called shruti, what is heard. Jaimini even meets an objection: parts of the Veda carry people's names. Those names, he answers, come from the ones who taught and recited those parts, not from authors. This is why Vedic chanting is guarded so fiercely. Students still learn each hymn by ear from a teacher, in patterns that repeat the words one by one and in pairs, so not one syllable slips. If no person made the words, no one's mistake is hiding in them, and no one edits them. Other Hindu schools see the Veda's origin differently, and the tradition keeps them all in the conversation. For Kumarila, one doubting if cost an eye.
screen: `THE WORDS MUST BE RELIABLE.` · `WORD AND MEANING, ORIGINAL.` · `SHRUTI: NOT MADE, BUT HEARD.` · `TEACHERS' NAMES, NOT AUTHORS.` · then, large: `NOT ONE SYLLABLE SLIPS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one line you were given and have never changed: a mantra, a blessing, a verse, a prayer from home. Say it once, slowly, exactly as it was taught to you, every syllable. If you pray, let that line be your prayer, and rest in the quiet after it. If you don't, notice what it feels like to say words you didn't write.
